subject: Biology
title: Problem Solving and Insight
description: A 60-second lesson on Problem Solving and Insight.

hook.text: A crow drops stones into a tube of water to raise the level and reach a floating treat.

buildup.text: Problem solving requires more than trial and error—it involves understanding cause and effect.

discovery.text: Kea parrots in New Zealand solve multi-step puzzles that stump many primates.

twist.text: Octopuses unscrew jar lids from the inside. They can solve mazes and remember solutions for months.

climax.text: Insight—suddenly grasping a solution without trial and error—has been demonstrated in apes and corvids.

punchline.text: Think first, act once. That's insight.

quiz.question: Which animal can unscrew jar lids from the inside?

details.summary: Some animals solve novel problems without trial and error, suggesting insight: the sudden understanding of a solution. New Caledonian crows craft multi-step tools, and great apes solve puzzles requiring mental simulation of outcomes before acting.
details.whyItMatters: Problem-solving and insight challenge assumptions that complex cognition requires human-level brains. Studying these abilities reveals the minimum neural requirements for flexible intelligence.
takeaways: New Caledonian crows manufacture and use multi-step tools
Great apes can plan solutions mentally before executing them
Insight-like behavior has been documented in birds, primates, and octopuses

faq.question: What is the best evidence of insight in animals?
faq.answer: New Caledonian crows that spontaneously combine two short sticks to make a tool long enough to reach food, having never seen this solution before, demonstrate insight. They appear to mentally simulate the solution before acting.

faq.question: How do researchers distinguish insight from trial and error?
faq.answer: Insight is characterized by sudden correct solutions without prior attempts, long pauses before acting, and immediate success. Trial and error involves repeated random attempts with gradual improvement. The speed and accuracy of first attempts indicate insight.
